figure: Figure 25.1 — The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record
issue: The supersession arrow is drawn from the bottom of the ADR-001 field stack (below the Alternatives box) rather than from the Consequences box it names, and the figure label asserts a relation the caption hedges.
evidence: The dashed red arrow is labeled 'consequences of ADR-001 become the context of ADR-002' but visually originates beneath the entire five-field stack (at/below the 'Alternatives / rejected options' box), not at the 'Consequences / the effects' box. The caption states the relation hedged and scoped: 'the Consequences of ADR-001 may become part of the Context of ADR-002', whereas the figure label states 'become the context' (unhedged, whole-field). The figure's whole point is the consequences→context handoff, so the drawn anchor is the semantic payload of the diagram.
root_cause: Arrow anchored to the record as a unit instead of to the specific field the label references; label wording simplified relative to the caption.
correction: Anchor the arrow's origin at the Consequences box (or draw a short connector from that box to the arrow), and align the label with the caption's hedged phrasing (e.g., 'consequences of ADR-001 feed the context of ADR-002'), keeping the [ILLUSTRATIVE] scope intact.
acceptance_test: On the rebuilt page, the arrow's top endpoint is level with the 'Consequences' box, and the figure label and caption express the same modality (both hedged or both definite); grayscale print of p. 395 still distinguishes ADR-001 from ADR-002 via the '(superseded)' / '(new — supersedes ADR-001)' text, which it currently does.

figure: Figure 25.1 — Anatomy of an ADR, and how one ADR supersedes the next
issue: The red dashed supersession arrow runs from the bottom edge of the whole ADR-001 box to the top edge of the whole ADR-002 box, not from the Consequences field to the Context field. The label says 'consequences of ADR-001 become the context of ADR-002', and the caption says 'the Consequences of ADR-001 may become part of the Context of ADR-002', but the drawn endpoints encode whole-record carryover rather than field-level carryover.
evidence: In the rendered figure, the arrow begins below the 'Alternatives' field of ADR-001 and terminates above 'Title & status' in ADR-002. The five fields are individually drawn, so the reader is invited to read field-level relationships; the arrow contradicts that granularity.
acceptance_test: Redraw the arrow so it originates at the 'Consequences' field of ADR-001 and terminates at the 'Context' field of ADR-002, or add short connector stubs from those two fields to the existing arrow. Re-render and confirm the arrow endpoints visibly attach to the named fields, not to the outer box edges.

issue: The dashed red connector between the two ADR records points the opposite way from its own label and from the caption. The arrowhead is at the TOP (into ADR-001), while the label and the caption both describe information flowing FROM ADR-001's Consequences INTO ADR-002's Context. A reader who follows the arrowhead concludes that the new ADR feeds the superseded one — the reverse of the intended lesson.
evidence: Rendered page: red dashed vertical segment between the ADR-001 bottom rule and the ADR-002 top rule, arrowhead at the upper end. Adjacent label: 'consequences of ADR-001 / became the context of ADR-002'. Caption: 'the Consequences of ADR-001 may become part of the Context of ADR-002, which supersedes it while the original stays on file.' The caption's own wording ('which supersedes it') is the only thing that could license an upward arrow, and it is not what the arrow is labelled.
acceptance_test: Re-render and confirm the arrowhead orientation from the source. Then either (a) reverse the arrow so it runs ADR-001 → ADR-002 and keep the label 'consequences of ADR-001 became the context of ADR-002', or (b) keep the upward arrow and relabel it 'ADR-002 supersedes ADR-001 (ADR-001 kept, not edited)'. Exactly one reading must survive caption + label + arrowhead together.

issue: The in-figure title ('Anatomy of an ADR, and how one ADR supersedes the next') restates the caption almost verbatim, and the two differ in wording ('ADR' vs 'Architecture Decision Record'), so the reader reads the same sentence twice and the caption contributes no interpretive content beyond the warning.
evidence: Rendered page: bold centered title above the diagram; caption below begins 'FIGURE 25.1: The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record, and how one ADR supersedes the next.'
acceptance_test: Delete the in-figure title and let the caption carry it, or replace the in-figure title with a one-line statement of the takeaway (e.g., 'A new ADR absorbs the old ADR's consequences as context; the old ADR is kept, not edited'). Acceptance: no sentence appears twice in near-identical form.

issue: Field-box text is set very small relative to the page: each of the five boxes carries a bold field name plus an italic gloss in a box roughly 0.25 in tall. The italic glosses ('the record', 'the situation', 'the choice', 'the effects', 'the rejected options') are the smallest text on the page and are the part of the figure that carries the caption's definitional content.
evidence: Rendered page at 150 dpi: each field box is ~18 px tall (~0.26 in) holding two lines of text; the italic gloss line is visibly smaller than the caption body type.
acceptance_test: Measure the rendered glyph sizes for the field names and glosses; raise any below 8 pt to ≥8 pt (gloss ≥8.5 pt italic), then re-render and confirm the five boxes still fit the card width without wrapping.

issue: Composition is left-heavy: the five field boxes occupy roughly the left fifth of each ADR card, leaving about three quarters of both cards empty, while the card headers are centered and the inter-record label floats in the resulting void. The reading order (centered header → far-left boxes) is not obvious, and the empty right half reads as unfinished rather than as deliberate whitespace.
evidence: Rendered page: field boxes span x≈90–175 of a ~415 px text block; the red label text sits at x≈205–330 with nothing to its right; both cards' rules span the full text width.
acceptance_test: Either widen the field boxes to fill the card (or lay the five fields out as a horizontal row within each card), or reduce the card width to the content and center the whole figure. Acceptance: the eye enters at the header and reaches the fields without a lateral jump, and no region of the figure is empty for more than one field-box width.

acceptance_test: Rebalance the column widths (narrow Workload/Input, widen the strategy column) or move the strategy column to a second line spanning the row; confirm no cell wraps to more than three lines and the table still fits the text block.

figure: Figure 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue: The in-figure title contains editorial meta-commentary — '(grouped bars, not radar)' — that is meaningless to a first-time reader, and the title otherwise near-duplicates the caption verbatim.
evidence: In-figure title: 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)'. Caption: 'FIGURE 26.1: Workload fingerprints on the six axes.' The word 'radar' appears nowhere in the visible text of pp. 424–425 (the provenance note on PDF 424 / printed 404 discusses axes and authored 0–1 scores but never mentions a radar chart), so the parenthetical reads as a note to a designer/reviewer that survived into the built PDF rather than reader-facing content.
root_cause: Production/review-response note left embedded in the figure title; title and caption carry the same information with no division of labor.
correction: Replace the title with reader-facing content (e.g., 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (authored intensity, 0–1)') and let the caption carry the explanatory load ('Grouped bars; compare within an axis, not across axes'), removing the chart-type meta-commentary.
acceptance_test: Grep the built PDF for 'not radar' and 'radar': zero hits outside any deliberate prose discussion; the figure title and caption no longer repeat the same phrase, and the legend note 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes' remains the sole statement of the comparison rule.

figure: Figure 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue: The legend swatches are solid color blocks, while the bars use hatch patterns (diagonal, crosshatch, dots). In grayscale, the solid legend swatches collapse to similar gray values and do not carry the pattern encoding used in the plot, so the legend cannot reliably map categories to bars without color.
evidence: The rendered legend shows three solid squares: blue for 'Long-context RAG Q&A', orange for 'High-throughput chat', green for 'Batch inference'. The corresponding bars are hatched. The chart's own note says 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes', but the legend does not preserve the non-color encoding that makes the bars distinguishable in grayscale.
acceptance_test: Add the matching hatch pattern to each legend swatch, or direct-label the three bars in each group. Re-render in grayscale and confirm a reader can map each bar to its category without relying on hue.

issue: Excessive whitespace and weak figure placement: the grouped-bar chart occupies only the middle band of the page, leaving large empty regions above (between the running header and the chart title) and below (between the caption and the footer), so the page reads as under-filled for a high-quality technical book.
evidence: Rendered page 405 shows the plot area at roughly 35–40% of page height with the legend and a one-line caption beneath it; the top ~25% and bottom ~25% of the page are blank. The chart is not large enough to justify a dedicated page at its current size. (Semantic content, hatching-based grayscale distinction, and axis labels are otherwise correct and legible.)
acceptance_test: Either enlarge the plot (taller bars, larger axis/legend type) so it fills ~70% of the page height, or pull the figure up to share the page with the §26.2.1 prose that introduces it (page 404). After the change, no single blank band should exceed ~15% of page height, and the caption must remain attached directly below the figure.

issue: The 'Traffic (rps)' category label attaches a physical unit to an axis whose values are authored 0–1 intensities. A reader glancing at the chart can read the bar heights as rps, which is the single most likely misreading of this figure.
evidence: Rendered page: x tick 'Traffic (rps)'; y axis 'Authored intensity (0–1)'; note 'per-axis 0–1 scale: compare within an axis, not across axes.'
acceptance_test: Change the tick label to 'Traffic volume' (or 'Traffic (rps) → intensity'), and confirm no other axis label carries a unit the 0–1 scale does not express.

issue: The in-figure title carries a design-process parenthetical — 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)' — that tells the reader about a chart type not used, and it duplicates the caption's subject rather than adding the takeaway.
evidence: Rendered page: chart title 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)'; caption 'FIGURE 26.1: Workload fingerprints on the six axes.'
acceptance_test: Remove '(grouped bars, not radar)' from the in-figure title; if the in-figure title is retained, make it state the takeaway (e.g., 'Each family peaks on a different axis') rather than restating the caption.

issue: Axis tick labels, category labels, legend entries and the italic note are all set smaller than the caption body type. The note ('per-axis 0–1 scale: compare within an axis, not across axes.') is the smallest text in the figure and carries the figure's most important interpretive caveat — the one that prevents the reader from comparing bar heights across axes.
evidence: Rendered page at 150 dpi: note text is visibly smaller than the caption's first line; tick labels ('0.0'…'1.0') are smaller than the legend text.
acceptance_test: Measure rendered sizes; bring all in-figure text to ≥8 pt (note ≥8.5 pt) and re-render; confirm the chart still fits the text block and the note remains on one line.

issue: The figure sits alone on a float page with roughly the top quarter and bottom quarter empty, and the chart itself is small relative to the text block. This under-fill is the direct cause of the sub-8 pt type noted above, and it separates the figure from the §26.2.1 matrix it visualizes.
evidence: Rendered page: running header at top, then blank space until the chart title at roughly 30% of page height; caption ends at roughly 70%.
acceptance_test: Enlarge the chart (taller plot area, larger fonts) to fill the text block, or move the figure onto the page carrying the §26.2.1 matrix so the reader can compare matrix rows and fingerprints side by side.

figure: Figure 26.1 — cross-reference from the Ch 26 mini-case
issue: The mini-case instructs the reader to 'read the capstone's workload against Fig 26.1', but the capstone matches none of the three families plotted. The capstone is a short-prompt (1,200-token), latency-sensitive, ~2 rps RAG workload; Fig 26.1 draws the RAG family with the HIGHEST context length (~0.95) and the LOWEST latency sensitivity (~0.40) — the opposite of the capstone — and the only family with high latency sensitivity (~0.90) is 'High-throughput chat', which the capstone is not (traffic ~0.95 vs. the capstone's ~2 rps). The instruction cannot be executed as written.
evidence: Printed p. 411: 'the architect reads the capstone's workload against Fig 26.1 — a short-prompt, latency-sensitive RAG workload, closest to the matrix's short-input/latency-bound rows'. Printed p. 405 figure: Long-context RAG Q&A context-length bar ≈0.95, latency-sensitivity bar ≈0.40; High-throughput chat latency-sensitivity bar ≈0.90, traffic bar ≈0.95.
acceptance_test: Either add a fourth family to Fig 26.1 matching the capstone's short-prompt/latency-bound profile, or rewrite the mini-case step to state explicitly that the capstone is a deliberate departure from all three plotted families and to name the §26.2.1 matrix row it does match. Acceptance: after reading, the reader can name the family the capstone matches, or state that none matches.

issue: The mini-case names the dominant constraint as a p99 TTFT target of ~80 ms, but never states whether the composed solution meets it. The modeled p99 is 250 ms (or 450 ms as printed) — 3–5× over target — and the mini-case ends without a verdict on the constraint it set out to locate. Fig 26.2's loop is drawn as closing on a 'validate' step with no criterion shown, so the figure implies a closed loop the prose never closes.
evidence: Printed p. 411: 'locate the dominant constraint: tail latency/queueing under the p99 ≈ 80 ms TTFT target'. Printed p. 414: 'under the hit-50 ms / miss-250 ms model p99 = 250 ms'. No sentence on either page states target met / not met.
acceptance_test: Add an explicit verdict to the mini-case (met / partially met / not met, with the residual gap and the next lever — e.g., inference sharding), and reflect that verdict in Fig 26.2's 'validate' step so the loop's exit condition is visible.

figure: Table, §26.8 (Cost row) + adjacent prose on the same page
issue: Cost-ledger arithmetic is internally inconsistent: the table's parenthetical base and the prose's rounded base both disagree with the table's own printed result and with the prose's unrounded value, so a reader cannot reproduce $0.0076 from the numbers shown next to it.
evidence: Table 'Modeled example' cell reads: '$0.0076 (API-basis marginal: $0.0164 × 0.65; self-host all-in is a separate basis, §26.8)'. But 0.0164 × 0.65 = 0.01066, not 0.0076. The printed 0.0076 actually equals 0.01164 × 0.65 = 0.007566. The prose on the same page reads: 'The hosted-API cost is a separate basis: $0.016/request (unrounded $0.01164 ≈ $11.6 per 1,000 requests, Ch 4)'. Here 0.01164 × 1000 = 11.64 ≈ 11.6 (consistent), but 0.01164 rounds to $0.012, not $0.016. Three per-request values (0.0164, 0.016, 0.01164) are therefore in play, and only 0.01164 reproduces the printed 0.0076. The table's stated multiplier base (0.0164) is the wrong anchor, and the prose's rounded figure ($0.016) is also wrong relative to its own unrounded figure.
acceptance_test: After the edit, recompute and confirm: (a) the table parenthetical reads '$0.01164 × 0.65' (or '$0.012 × 0.65 ≈ $0.0076') so that base × 0.65 = 0.0076; (b) the prose rounded value is '$0.012/request' or the rounded figure is dropped in favor of '$0.01164'; (c) 0.01164 × 0.65 = 0.007566 ≈ 0.0076 and 0.01164 × 1000 = 11.64 ≈ 11.6. All three anchors (table result, table base, prose base) must then agree, and the FACT Target '< $0.015' must still be satisfied by 0.0076.

issue: The parenthetical '(~4% of the ~450 ms uncached baseline, not a blended average)' is attached to 'p99 TTFT ~450 ms', which is 100% of the ~450 ms uncached baseline, not ~4%. The only quantity in the sentence that is a plausible source of a dropped digit is the mean (~180 ms ≈ 40% of 450 ms). As printed, the figure's takeaway carries a percentage that no stated quantity satisfies.
evidence: Printed p. 414 as quoted. 180/450 = 40%; 450/450 = 100%; no quantity in the sentence equals ~4% of 450 ms (18 ms) or of any other baseline stated on the page.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the parenthetical so it annotates the mean (e.g., 'mean ~180 ms ≈ 40% of the ~450 ms uncached baseline') and delete or re-derive the '~4%' figure; verify the corrected percentage against the §26.8 arithmetic.

figure: Table — Ch 26 mini-case results table, 'Cost' row
issue: The 'Modeled example' cell ends with '$26.8', where the parallel cell in the 'Configuration' column uses '§26.8'. Inside a cost table a bare '$26.8' reads as a dollar amount, not a section reference, and it sits next to '$0.0076', '$0.0116' and '$26.8' — three dollar-prefixed tokens in one cell.
evidence: Rendered page: Configuration cell 'DERIVED from FACT inputs, §26.8 — not itself a FACT'; Modeled example cell '$0.0076 (API-basis marginal; $0.0116 × 0.65; self-host all-in is a separate basis, $26.8)'.
acceptance_test: Replace '$26.8' with '§26.8' and re-render; then grep the table for any other '$' + digits sequence intended as a section reference.

page: PDF 434 / printed 414 (figure itself on PDF 435 / printed 415)
issue: The takeaway attached to Fig 26.2 states two mutually exclusive p99 values in one sentence: 'p99 TTFT ~450 ms' and, in the same sentence's scope clause, 'under the hit-50 ms / miss-250 ms model p99 = 250 ms'. Under the stated two-point model (35% hit at 50 ms, 65% miss at 250 ms) the p99 is 250 ms, so the printed '~450 ms' is the UNCACHED baseline, not the composed result. The figure's box 1 uses the same 450 ms number for the baseline assumption, so the figure and its takeaway assign the same number two different meanings.
evidence: Printed p. 414: 'the three patterns compose to mean TTFT ~180 ms and p99 TTFT ~450 ms (~4% of the ~450 ms uncached baseline, not a blended average) … Scope: full arithmetic in §26.8; weighted average of component latencies is a mean, not a quantile — under the hit-50 ms / miss-250 ms model p99 = 250 ms.' Independent recomputation: mean = 0.35×50 + 0.65×250 = 180 ms (mean is correct); p99 = 250 ms because 65% of requests are misses. Fig 26.2 box 1: 'scenario TTFT p99 ~450 ms' labelled ASSUMPTION.
acceptance_test: Recompute in §26.8 and print exactly one p99: 'mean TTFT ~180 ms and p99 TTFT ~250 ms'. Change Fig 26.2 box 1 to 'baseline (uncached) TTFT p99 ~450 ms' so the assumption and the result are not the same number, and confirm the takeaway's percentage clause annotates the quantity it follows.
